newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl and Yeltsin start talks amid tough rhetoric. [CORRECTED 13:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Kohl and Yeltsin start talks amid tough rhetoric. [CORRECTED 13:00 GMT]

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Russian President Boris Yeltsin began a one-day summit on Thursday amid tough talk from Moscow on the terms it would set for a planned charter on relations with NATO.

Yeltsin looked pale and seemed tired as Kohl welcomed him at his hotel in the stately spa resort of Baden-Baden. The chancellor occasionally seemed to have to guide his avowed friend as they posed for photographs.

But the Kremlin leader was more animated as he told local people, "Nice town you've got here". He even performed a brief mime of marching in a parade as he assured them there would be no undue pomp during his visit to a town whose casino was immortalised in Dostoyevsky's 19th-century novel "The Gambler".
Yeltsin's programme had said the two men would take a five-minute walk from the hotel to the park where he was received with military honours, but in the event they drove.

The discussions, taking place over a lengthy working lunch at a nearby country restaurant, were likely to focus on attempts to secure an agreement between NATO and Russia which gives Moscow influence on the alliance as it expands eastwards.

Neither man made any comment to reporters, but on the eve of the talks Yeltsin's spokesman had harsh words for NATO, warning Moscow would reject a treaty that is in the works if it did not guarantee the alliance would not move troops and arms eastwards.
Through all the criticism Yeltsin has suffered and through his heart operation last year and pneumonia this year, his most constant supporter in the West has been Helmut Kohl.

Presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky (corrects to insert first name and title) said the president was now hoping for help from Kohl in reaching a compromise with NATO at this meeting, their fifth in just over a year. But the tone of his media briefing on Wednesday night had a hard edge.

Yeltsin was to brief Kohl on his Helsinki summit last month with U.S. President Bill Clinton, which laid the groundwork for efforts to draw up a treaty or "charter" between Russia and NATO that would give Moscow some say in the alliance as it extends membership to some former Soviet bloc states.

But Yastrzhembsky said the signing of a treaty was by no means a foregone conclusion and the expansion of NATO into eastern Europe remained, in Moscow's view, "the West's biggest historic mistake since the end of the Cold War".

Russia has made it clear it does not want Western troops and weapons moving closer to its borders. NATO, however, does not want new members -- set to be invited to join in July -- to lack the defence guarantees of existing partners.
"Without binding and concrete terms in the treaty on military issues, there would scarcely be any point in Russia signing such a document," Yastrzhembsky said.
The chairman of NATO's military committee, German general Klaus Naumann, said NATO had no intention of pledging not to instal command or air defence installations on the territory of new members.

There appeared to be little prospect of major progress in the most thorny bilateral issue between Russia and Germany -- the fate of thousands of priceless works of art seized by Soviet troops from occupied Germany at the end of World War Two.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had brought a valuable piece of treasure for Kohl, but there was no word on what it was.

German officials made clear they expected little more than a token gesture from Yeltsin, who has been unable to prevent Russia's communist-led parliament trying to declare the art works inalienable Russian property.

Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin was keen on a proposal from Kohl for a joint exhibition tour of the best captured art. But he said Germany's Western allies like Britain and the United States should also be asked to show captured treasures that they held.

Yeltsin, in turn, would ask Kohl to return property to the Russian Orthodox Church -- including an onion-domed Russian church in Baden-Baden. Hitler handed the property to the church formed by Russian exiles who fled the 1917 Bolshevik revolution.
